senses.d: A one-room Native American (especially Navajo) dwelling or lodge, constructed of wood and earth and covered with mud.

ety.text: From Middle English hog, from Old English hogg, hocg (“hog”), possibly from Old Norse hǫggva (“to strike, chop, cut”), from Proto-Germanic *hawwaną (“to hew, forge”), from Proto-Indo-European *kewh₂- (“to beat, hew, forge”). Cognate with Old High German houwan, Old Saxon hauwan, Old English hēawan (English hew). Hog originally meant a castrated male pig, hence a sense of “the cut one”. (Compare hogget for a castrated male sheep.) More at hew.

senses.d: Any animal belonging to the Suidae family of mammals, especially the pig, the warthog, and the boar.
An adult swine, at or above a certain body weight.
A greedy person or thing; one who refuses to share; a gluttonous one.
ex: Since the latest upgrade, this program has turned into a CPU hog.

senses.d: A large motorcycle, particularly a Harley-Davidson.
A young sheep that has not been shorn.
A rough, flat scrubbing broom for scrubbing a ship's bottom under water.
A device for mixing and stirring the pulp from which paper is made.
A shilling coin; its value, 12 old pence.
ex: hog (pl hog). A shilling: orig. (ca 1670), c.; in C.19–20, low s.

senses.d: A tanner, a sixpence coin; its value.
ex: hog (pl hog)... 2. In C.18–early 19, occ. a sixpence: also c., whence the U.S. sense. Prob. ex the figure of a hog on a small silver coin.

senses.d: A half-crown coin; its value, 30 old pence.
To greedily take more than one's share, to take precedence at the expense of another or others.
ex: Hey! Quit hogging all the blankets.

senses.d: To clip the mane of a horse, making it short and bristly.
ex: Some, perhaps, would wish to plait or shave the tail and crimp or hog the mane to complete the picture.

senses.d: (of a hedge) to trim up closely
To scrub with a hog, or scrubbing broom.
To cause the keel of a ship to arch upwards (the opposite of sag).
To take a rough cut, quickly removing material; to hog out.
To process (bark, etc.) into hog fuel.

grp.label: to take more than one's share

ety.text: Originally imitative of the noise a pig makes.

Inherited from Old Spanish puerco, from Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”). The "police officer" slang sense is apparently a semantic loan from English pig.

pt:ganancioso.gl: greedy (having greed; consumed by selfish desires)
